title: Held down, never killed
hook: under the planted foot lies a small figure, ignorance itself, and the dancer never finishes him off
carry: the real enemy is ignorance, held down by remembering
tomorrow: why is there a river in Shiva's hair?

segments.voice: Yesterday: his lifted foot is grace; refuge is at his feet. That's where the elephant hand points, and where Hindus bow. Today, the other foot, and who's under it.
screen: `GRACE IS THERE. BOW THERE.` · `TODAY: UNDER THE FOOT.`

segments.voice: He's the easiest part of the image to miss. Look down past the swinging arms and the flying hair to Nataraja's right foot, the planted one. Under it, flat on his belly, lies a small, round-limbed figure, often holding a snake, pinned to the ground. He isn't the hero of anything. He's closer to the name that was right there a second ago, or the reason you walked into this room: gone. Small, daily, and always back. His name is Apasmara.
screen: `EASY TO MISS.` → `UNDER THE PLANTED FOOT.` → `HIS NAME: APASMARA.`

segments.voice: In the usual reading, Apasmara is ignorance: the forgetting that hides what's true. Hindu teachers have a word for it, avidya, not-knowing, and in much of Hindu thought it's the root trouble, deeper than any enemy outside you: forgetting who you really are, and forgetting God. There's a story behind him, told in the temple tradition of Chidambaram and retold by the art historian Ananda Coomaraswamy. In a forest lived a community of sages, proud of their own rites, who thought they had no need of Shiva. He came among them in disguise, and they were furious, so they used their powers against him. First they sent a tiger. Shiva caught it, peeled off its skin, and wore it at his waist. Then a snake: he hung it around his neck like a garland. Then a dwarf, a malicious little creature. Shiva put his foot on its back and began to dance, and the sages, watching, gave up their pride. Here's the detail worth keeping. Shiva never kills Apasmara. He keeps him under the foot, and keeps dancing. Many teachers read that as honest: ignorance doesn't vanish for good in one blow. It's held down, again and again, by remembering. That's why so much Hindu practice is repetition: a name said on every bead of a mala, a lamp lit every evening, the same prayer before every meal. Each one is the foot pressing down again. Remembering isn't a victory you win once. It's a step you keep taking.
screen: `APASMARA: IGNORANCE, AVIDYA.` · `TIGER, SNAKE, DWARF FROM THE SAGES.` · `HE IS HELD DOWN, NEVER KILLED.` · `WHY HINDU PRACTICE REPEATS.` · then, large: `REMEMBERING IS A STEP YOU KEEP TAKING.`

segments.voice: With both feet flat on the floor, rest your attention in the right foot: the heel, the ball, the toes. When the mind wanders off into a plan or a memory, that's Apasmara, and it's fine: press the right foot gently into the floor and come back. If you pray, say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, each time you come back, the way a mala is told bead by bead; if not, just say here.
Apasmara, under the planted foot: ignorance, avidya, held down and never killed, so that remembering stays a step the dancer keeps taking.
Your line: the real enemy is ignorance, held down by remembering. When forgetting comes back, press down again, gently. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Nataraja images the right foot rests on Apasmara, a small figure read as ignorance or forgetfulness; the story of the forest sages, the tiger, the snake and the dwarf is told in the temple tradition of Chidambaram. Repeated practices, such as japa on a mala and the daily lamp, are often explained as remembering again and again.

notes: The forest-sages story (often the Daruka or Taruka forest; tiger, snake, dwarf) follows Coomaraswamy's retelling in 'The Dance of Shiva', which cites the Koyil Puranam. Some tellings add a deer, fire or other attacks; kept to three. Confirm.

Apasmara 'linked with forgetting': the Sanskrit lexicon gives forgetfulness, loss of memory and epilepsy for apasmara. Confirm wording. Tamil name given as Muyalakan (also Muyalaka); confirm spelling.
'Often holding a snake' describes many bronzes; confirm.
The two readings of why Apasmara isn't killed are framed as 'some readers'; they are popular interpretations, not from a cited text.
